6.9 Retirement Planning

How much is needed

Section titled “How much is needed”

Retirement planning starts from spending: how much is needed each year in retirement (in today’s purchasing power), how much of it Social Security, pensions and other steady income will provide, and the remaining gap, which the portfolio must fill.

Spending in retirement is usually lower than income before it: there is no more saving for retirement, no payroll tax, and fewer work-related costs. A common rule of thumb is that retirement spending is about 70% to 85% of pre-retirement income; this share is the replacement ratio, but it varies widely between households: health spending rises with age, travel and similar spending may be higher early in retirement, and whether the mortgage is paid off matters a lot.

Check C1
A household earns 200,000 dollars a year before tax, puts 30,000 dollars a year into retirement accounts, and will pay off its mortgage at retirement. Which of the following is least likely a reason that spending after retirement is lower than income before it?
Is retirement saving still needed after retiring? Was this part of income spent or saved before?
Payroll tax applies only to wages; once the mortgage is paid off, are monthly payments still needed?

Withdrawal rates and the “4% rule”

Section titled “Withdrawal rates and the “4% rule””

Once the gap is known, the assets needed depend on how much can safely be taken from the portfolio each year. Bengen (1994) tested this with US historical data from 1926: withdraw a share of the portfolio in the first year of retirement, raise that amount with inflation every year after, hold 50% to 75% in stocks, and continue for 30 years. He found that with an initial withdrawal rate of about 4%, the money never ran out for any historical starting year. The “Trinity study” of Cooley, Hubbard and Walz (1998) reached a similar conclusion. This is the well-known “4% rule”, which gives one kind of safe withdrawal rate.

The result rests on important assumptions: the data are from the US, whose stock market was among the world’s best in the 20th century; the horizon is 30 years; no fees or taxes are deducted; and real spending is fixed each year, not adjusted to markets. Based on current valuations and rates, Morningstar estimates that for people retiring in 2026 with 30% to 50% in stocks, the initial withdrawal rate with a 90% chance of lasting 30 years is about 3.9% (2025 research). People willing to cut spending when markets fall can start at a higher rate.

Check C2
Under the "4% rule", a retiree withdraws 4% of the portfolio's value at the start of each year.
In Bengen's study, how is the amount withdrawn in the second and later years set? Does it depend on that year's portfolio value?

Sequence-of-returns risk

Section titled “Sequence-of-returns risk”

While saving, the order of yearly returns does not affect final wealth as long as the returns are the same: the order of multiplication does not matter. With withdrawals it is different. Sequence-of-returns risk is the risk that the same set of returns, arriving in a different order, gives very different results for a portfolio being drawn down.

Check C3

Both cases have 29 years of 5% and one year of −30%. Are the average returns the same?
In the figure the fall is always 30%. Where does the difference come from?

When to claim Social Security

Section titled “When to claim Social Security”

US Social Security benefits can start at any age from 62 to 70. For people born in 1960 or later, the full retirement age is 67: starting at 67 gives the full benefit; starting at 62 reduces the monthly amount by 30%; each year of delay adds 8%, reaching 124% of the full benefit at 70. Benefits are adjusted for inflation each year (by 2.8% in 2026) and paid for life; when one spouse dies, the other can receive the larger of the two benefits.

Social Security’s finances should also be considered: according to the Trustees Report released in June 2026, the retirement trust fund is projected to run out in the fourth quarter of 2032, after which, unless Congress acts, continuing income would pay only about 78% of scheduled benefits.

Check C4
A healthy couple aged 62; the husband's Social Security benefit is far higher than the wife's. For the household as a whole, delaying to 70 is most valuable for:
After the husband dies, whose benefit does the wife receive? Delaying which benefit raises the income of whoever lives longer?
According to the report, about 78% would still be paid after the fund runs out. How much does claiming early cut? Does that erase the gain from delaying?

Longevity risk and annuities

Section titled “Longevity risk and annuities”

Another risk in retirement planning is living longer than expected: longevity risk. Life expectancy is only an average: for a couple aged 65, the chance that at least one lives past 90 is far from small. Planning for average life expectancy means a large chance that the money runs short.

Ways to deal with longevity risk include: delaying Social Security (itself an inflation-adjusted lifetime income); buying an immediate annuity, paying an insurer a lump sum in exchange for regular payments for life; and leaving room in the withdrawal plan. An annuity pools many people’s longevity risk: money left by those who die early pays those who live long; this is called the mortality credit.

Check C5
A 65-year-old retiree has a life expectancy of 85, so he needs only enough money to last 20 years.
Life expectancy is an average. How likely is it that he lives beyond it? What happens if the money runs out at 85 and he lives to 95?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Retirement planning starts from the spending gap; replacement ratios are often 70% to 85%, but vary by household.
  • The “4% rule” rests on US historical data, a 30-year horizon and fixed real spending; at current valuations some research puts it at about 3.9%.
  • With withdrawals, the same returns in a different order give very different results; falls early in retirement do the most harm.
  • Social Security can start from 62 to 70, rising 8% for each year of delay, adjusted for inflation and paid for life.
  • Longevity risk can be met by delaying Social Security, annuities and a conservative withdrawal plan.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A couple aged 60 plans to retire at 65 and needs 100,000 dollars a year (in today's purchasing power) in retirement. Their combined Social Security at 67 will be 45,000 dollars a year; for simplicity assume this income starts at retirement, with no other pension. Ignore taxes.
(a) At initial withdrawal rates of 3.5% and 4%, how large must the portfolio be (thousand dollars)?
(b) They say: "The 4% rule shows that 1 million dollars is enough to retire safely." Evaluate this statement. When might 4% be too high? What adjustments could they make?
Question 2
Two retirees each have 1,000 (thousand dollars) and withdraw 50 at the start of each year; their returns over three years are: A −20%, +10%, +30%; B +30%, +10%, −20%.
(a) How much does each have left after three years?
(b) An adviser says: "Their three returns are exactly the same, just in a different order; the arithmetic and geometric means are equal, so the results should be the same." Evaluate this statement. What if neither withdrew anything? What does this imply for the asset allocation of people near retirement?
Question 3
A single person can receive 2,100 dollars a month starting at 62, or 3,720 dollars a month starting at 70 (both in today's purchasing power, adjusted for inflation afterwards).
(a) Ignoring discounting, at what age are the cumulative totals of the two choices equal?
(b) He says: "Many people don't live to 80, so claiming early is better." Evaluate this statement, considering discounting, longevity risk, and what he lives on while delaying.
Question 4
A 65-year-old retiree has 500,000 dollars. Option one: buy an immediate life annuity paying a fixed 7% a year (nominal, not adjusted for inflation). Option two: invest it himself and withdraw at an initial rate of 4%, raised with inflation afterwards. Inflation is 3% a year.
(a) How much does option one pay each year (thousand dollars)? Roughly what is that payment worth in today's purchasing power after 20 years? How much does option two withdraw in the first year?
(b) His friend says: "An annuity is a bad deal: if you die early, the insurer keeps all the money." Evaluate this statement, and compare the risks of the two options.
